title: Undertow and Interior
premise: Emrys Ashgrove, a translator who has spent thirty years burying his childhood in a Welsh-speaking coastal village, hears a song on a late-night radio program that was never recorded — a song his brother Idris wrote the summer before he drowned. The broadcast means someone else remembers, and Emrys's careful silence begins to crack. As he returns to the village to close the sale of the family house, he uncovers what really happened the night Idris died: not an accident alone, but a secret kept by the two people who loved him most. To survive the truth, Emrys must finally speak — in the language he is losing, out loud, before the house and everything in it passes to strangers.
about_author: Astrid Eriksen grew up between a fishing town in western Norway and her grandmother's farm in Carmarthenshire, a childhood spent translating herself for both households. She worked as a literary translator for fifteen years before writing fiction of her own; Undertow and Interior is her second novel.

chapters.title: The Smile That Ends Conversations
chapters.summary: Emrys, 54, works in London translating Norwegian crime novels while his Welsh erodes word by word. A dinner party scene shows his perfected deflections. When a caller on late-night radio hums an unrecorded song — one only Idris ever wrote — Emrys drops his glass. POV: Emrys. Beat: the buried past knocks.

chapters.title: A Song With No Recording
chapters.summary: Emrys replays the broadcast obsessively, confirming details only he and Idris could know: the wrong chord, the joke about the gulls. He contacts the station; the caller left no name. His partner Nia notices him slipping into Welsh in his sleep. POV: Emrys. Beat: denial gives way to compulsion.

chapters.title: Probate and Salt Air
chapters.summary: Emrys travels to the village to finalize the house sale, telling himself it's practical. The estate agent, Bronwen, is a girl he once knew; she treats him with a warmth that feels like accusation. The house smells of forty years of held breath. POV: Emrys. Beat: return as trespass.

chapters.title: What the House Keeps
chapters.summary: Sorting belongings, Emrys finds Idris's notebook of songs, water-damaged, the radio song among them with a second verse he never knew. A photograph shows Idris with Carys Vaughan, Emrys's first love, the summer of the drowning. POV: Emrys, with flashback fragments. Beat: evidence that memory lied to him.

chapters.title: Carys at the Chapel Gate
chapters.summary: Emrys seeks out Carys, now the village postmistress, expecting evasion. Instead she says, calmly, 'I wondered when you'd come.' She refuses to explain yet, insisting some things are said properly, in the right place. POV: Emrys. Beat: the gate opens but not the door.

chapters.title: Bronwen's Ledger
chapters.summary: Bronwen reveals the house sale has a complication: an anonymous buyer's clause delaying completion — someone wants time inside the house too. Emrys suspects Carys. His solicitor urges speed; something in him resists. POV: Emrys. Beat: the deadline becomes a character.

chapters.title: The Drowned Summer
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter, young Emrys's POV: the golden summer when Idris wrote songs, Carys listened, and Emrys translated everyone's feelings because he couldn't voice his own. Ends the night Idris went out in the boat. Beat: love triangle rendered as loyalty, not romance.

chapters.title: Nia Calls It Grief
chapters.summary: Back in London briefly, Nia confronts Emrys about his disappearances and his slipping language. He can't explain without confessing things he's never said aloud. They fight; she names his pattern: 'You translate so you never have to speak.' POV: Nia. Beat: the cost of silence made visible.

chapters.title: The Second Verse
chapters.summary: In the house, Emrys deciphers the water-blurred second verse — addressed to someone who promised to keep a secret 'under the water.' He realizes the song is a confession, and that Idris knew he might die. POV: Emrys. Beat: grief reorganizes into dread.

chapters.title: Old Men by the Harbour Wall
chapters.summary: Emrys buys drinks for the surviving fishermen of that summer. One, Ifor, drunk and kind, lets slip that the boat's bailer was missing that night — taken out deliberately. He clams up when Carys enters the pub. POV: Emrys. Beat: the accident theory cracks.

chapters.title: Carys's Version
chapters.summary: Carys finally talks: she and Idris were going to run away together; Emrys, unknowingly, told their parents about the plan to protect Idris from himself. Idris felt betrayed by the person he trusted most. POV: alternating Emrys and Carys. Beat: Emrys learns he was the wound.

chapters.title: Under the Water
chapters.summary: The full secret surfaces: Idris took the boat out intending to scare everyone, to force the family to let him go; the storm turned it real. Carys reached the shore too late and chose silence to protect Idris's memory — and Emrys from guilt. POV: Carys. Beat: truth arrives, heavy as seawater.

chapters.title: The Anonymous Buyer
chapters.summary: Bronwen discloses the delayed buyer: Ifor, who has been paying to keep the house unsold for years, believing Idris hid something in it. Emrys realizes three people have been circling the same silence for decades. POV: Emrys. Beat: private grief revealed as communal.

chapters.title: What Idris Hid
chapters.summary: Guided by the song's imagery, Emrys searches the house: under floorboards in Idris's room, letters — unsent, addressed to Emrys — written the week he died, forgiving him before Emrys even knew he'd sinned. POV: Emrys. Beat: absolution found where he least deserved it.

chapters.title: Loyalty Weighs Its Coin
chapters.summary: Ifor confronts Emrys, angry that the letters change nothing for him: his own brother lost his livelihood over that night's aftermath. Loyalty to the dead vs. truth for the living becomes the village's fault line. POV: Emrys. Beat: justice outside the law takes shape.

chapters.title: The Sale Signing
chapters.summary: The completion date arrives. Emrys sits across from Ifor at the solicitor's office, pen hovering, and asks for one week. Ifor, seeing the letters' effect on him, unexpectedly agrees — one week, no more. POV: Emrys. Beat: mercy from an unexpected quarter.

chapters.title: Learning the Words Again
chapters.summary: Emrys spends days relearning Welsh from Carys and an old hymnal, practicing aloud what he must say. Words come back like tide-borne objects, some broken. Nia arrives unannounced, choosing to witness rather than punish. POV: Emrys. Beat: preparation as penance.

chapters.title: The Empty House Speaks
chapters.summary: The night before the handover, Emrys stays alone in the house. He reads Idris's letters aloud in Welsh, voice failing and recovering, room by room. The house seems to answer in creaks and settling beams. POV: Emrys. Beat: the goodbye begins.

chapters.title: Out Loud, Before Witnesses
chapters.summary: At dawn, Emrys stands on the shore with Carys, Ifor, Bronwen, and Nia, and speaks the whole truth publicly — his betrayal, Idris's intention, the years of silence — in Welsh, then translates it into English himself, deliberately. POV: Emrys. Beat: climax; speech as both confession and release.

chapters.title: Justice Without a Courtroom
chapters.summary: Consequences ripple gently: Ifor donates part of the sale to restore the memorial stone with Idris's name spelled correctly; Carys retires the secret she's carried since nineteen. No laws were broken, but something is set right. POV: rotating village voices. Beat: communal exhale.

chapters.title: Keys on the Kitchen Table
chapters.summary: Emrys hands over the keys, leaving Idris's notebook open on the table to the finished song, now complete with its second verse. He keeps only one page: the letter beginning 'Dear Emrys, you were never the reason.' POV: Emrys. Beat: letting go without erasure.

chapters.title: Undertow and Interior
chapters.summary: Months later, Emrys and Nia walk a London street when the song plays again on a busker's guitar — someone learned it from the memorial service. Emrys smiles, the old conversation-ending smile, then lets it become a real one and sings along, badly, in Welsh. POV: Emrys. Beat: the language survives because he finally used it.
